title: Automatic standard building category classification from smart meter data – A supervised learning approach
tldr: Presents a supervised learning method with 82 physics-based features to classify buildings into standard Norwegian categories and heating type from hourly smart meter data, achieving 84% accuracy on a dataset of 2724 buildings.
problem_and_motivation: Metadata such as building category and heating type is often unavailable for smart meter data, yet it is valuable for grid planning and energy efficiency. Manual collection is difficult and time-consuming, and existing unsupervised methods do not align with standard building categories.
approach: Extracts 82 physics-based domain features from hourly electricity and temperature time series for each building.
Features are grouped into non-normalized load, load variation, seasonal differences, average daily profile, and standard load profile correlation.
Evaluates Decision Tree, Random Forest, SVM, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost, and CatBoost classifiers on a dataset of 2724 buildings.
Uses an 80/20 train-test split and performance metrics including accuracy, top-2 accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.
Compares the best supervised models against unsupervised K-means clustering and ensemble soft-voting methods.
Tests generalizability on three external datasets: iFlex (Norway), HUE (Canada), and BDG2 (USA/UK).
findings: Random Forest and CatBoost classifiers achieved 84% accuracy for building type (category + heating type) and 92% top-2 accuracy.
num: 89% accuracy was achieved when predicting building category alone, without heating type.
num: Forward Sequential Feature Selection identified 7-12 key features; accuracy peaked at approximately 86% with the top 9 features.
Supervised classification outperformed unsupervised K-means clustering for assigning standard building category labels.
The method generalized well to Norwegian residential buildings (70-75% accuracy on iFlex) but poorly to buildings from other climate zones (HUE: 46%, BDG2: 20%).
Soft-voting ensemble learning did not improve performance over the best individual classifiers.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a novel supervised classification framework for extracting standardized building metadata from smart meter data. It introduces 82 physics-based features designed to capture seasonal, daily, and temperature-dependent patterns in electricity consumption. The study provides a large-scale benchmark with 2724 buildings across 10 categories, demonstrating that supervised learning can outperform unsupervised clustering for this task. It also evaluates feature selection and generalizability across climates, advancing the methodology for building load profile classification.
directly_justifies: No existing method classifies standard building category and heating type from smart meter data alone.
Supervised classification achieved 84% accuracy, outperforming unsupervised clustering.
Feature selection reduced features to 7-12 while maintaining high accuracy.
The method is generalizable to other Norwegian buildings but not to other climate zones.
limits: Labels have uncertainty due to varied collection methods and potential building use changes.
Method cannot recognize building categories not present in the training set.
Transferability to other climate zones was poor, requiring additional features.
Tested on Norwegian data only; results may not generalize to other countries without retraining.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan across all topic domains was performed. The paper's core contribution—a supervised classification method for time-series data—maps primarily to topic 12.B (evaluation of algorithmic modules) and 6.A (predictive modeling). Topic 12.A is relevant due to the use of standard performance metrics. Topic 4.A and 4.B are contextual, as the paper identifies a gap in existing systems and motivates the need for metadata. Topics related to financial behavior, budgeting, anomaly detection, mobile design, and user engagement were considered but rejected as the paper focuses on building energy classification, not personal finance behavior or system design. The paper's application domain (buildings) is analogous to financial data in terms of time-series classification, but the specific problem is not directly about personal finance. Overall, the paper's relevance is strongest to algorithmic evaluation and modeling, with contextual ties to system landscapes and gaps.
